1:
Between the last chapter and this a space of years opens, and the witnesses begin by measuring it. The reformed John Gill sets the phrase “after these things” after Esther's marriage and after Mordecai's discovery of the plot against the king's life, reckoning with Aben Ezra that more than four years, perhaps five, had passed before Haman's sudden rise. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix on the elevation itself: Ahasuerus promoted Haman above all the princes that were with him, setting his seat higher than every other officer of the realm.

The puritan Matthew Henry turns the promotion over with a moralist's eye. Ahasuerus had lately taken Esther to his bosom, yet she had no such interest with him as to prevent the advancement of one she knew to be an enemy of her people — a reminder that when the good become great they still find they cannot do all the good, nor prevent all the mischief, they would. Henry wonders aloud what the king saw in Haman that was commendable: not honour, not justice, not any steady courage, but a man proud, passionate, and revengeful; and yet he was caressed and made the confidant and prime minister, while all the court adored the rising sun. “Princes' darlings,” he observes drily, “are not always worthies.”

The sharpest question is what “the Agagite” means, and here the witnesses divide. The wesleyan voices take it at face value: Adam Clarke supposes Haman a descendant of that Agag, king of the Amalekites, whom Saul spared but Samuel destroyed, and finds in this the root of his antipathy to the Jews; John Wesley calls him plainly an Amalekite of the royal seed whose kings were successively named Agag. Henry agrees, and Keil lets the title stand. But the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses a difficulty: nothing is known of Haman outside this book, and his name, with those of his father and his sons, is Persian, so that the descent from Agag — assumed since Josephus and the Targum called him an Amalekite — is hard to credit, both because of the Persian name and because after the wholesale destruction of Amalek in 1 Sam. 15 it is difficult to see how the kingly family could have survived, keeping a distinct tribal name for centuries. He notes that one Greek addition to the book calls Haman a Macedonian instead. Henry, for his part, draws the older identification into the drama of the whole story, recalling that Agag was a common style of the princes of Amalek in Num. 24:7, and that some thought Haman a prince by birth, his seat set above the rest as Jehoiakim's was above the captive kings in 2 Kings 25:28. So the chapter's villain enters already trailing an ancient quarrel, whether by blood or only by type.
2:
The command goes out and the whole court obeys, all but one. The reformed John Gill notes that the king's servants “in the gate” were not doorkeepers but courtiers, the officers who attended the palace; the wesleyan Adam Clarke agrees they were a higher class of officers, Mordecai among them, come to the gate to receive the king's commands. All of these knelt and did Haman reverence, for so the king had commanded — but Mordecai bowed not.

Why he would not is the question every witness feels, and they answer it together: the homage demanded was not mere civility but something like worship. Clarke weighs the two Hebrew verbs and finds the point in them. To bow (kara) is a civil courtesy that no Jewish law forbade, and to refuse it would have been mere obstinacy; but Haman looked for the prostration (shachah) that flings a man flat upon the earth — the highest reverence that can be paid to God or man — and the Targum even reports that he had set up a statue of himself before which all must fall. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase “did not prostrate himself,” the ordinary Eastern practice, and judges the objection to have been mainly religious, an unwillingness to give a man divine honours, since it draws from Mordecai the confession that he was a Jew. John Wesley reasons the same way from the very superfluity of the order: a merely civil respect to so great a prince needed no express command, so a divine honour must be meant; and it is no wonder a Jew refused it, when even the Greeks would not so adore the Persian kings themselves, and one Timocrates was put to death at Athens for prostrating himself before Darius.

Keil and Delitzsch add that falling to the earth before a king was in itself familiar enough among Israelites, as before the princes of Israel in 2 Sam. 18:28 and 1 Kings 1:16, so that the ground of the refusal must lie in the peculiar notions the Persians bound up with the act. The puritan Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a portrait of conscience under pressure. Mordecai's refusal, whatever the courtiers made of it, was pious and pleasing to God: religion forbade him to render to a mortal, and to so wicked a mortal, honours that savoured of idolatry, and it forbade him to flatter an Amalekite of that devoted nation with which God had sworn perpetual war. Religion does not destroy good manners, Henry allows — it teaches us to render honour where honour is due — yet a citizen of Zion, in his heart and in his very eyes, holds such a vile person cheap, as in Ps. 15:4.
3:
Before Haman himself takes notice, the court does. The reformed John Gill pictures the king's servants in the gate watching Mordecai's carriage toward Haman day after day, until curiosity turns to challenge. Their question — “Why transgressest thou the king's commandment?” — the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read as a daily, wearing interrogation: the other officials asked him from one day to the next why he set the royal order at nought, and he gave no heed to their words. When at last they reported the matter to Haman, it was “to see whether Mordecai's words would stand”; for he had told them the reason of his refusal, that he was a Jew.

That answer, Keil observes, is the hinge of the whole scene. Mordecai had not pleaded pride or private grievance but conscience: as a Jew he could not render to a man the honour that belonged to God alone. And lest the excuse seem a mere pretext, Keil is careful to note that prostration before an exalted person, and before a king above all, was no strange thing to Israelites — they had bowed so before their own princes — so that what Mordecai balked at was not the posture itself but the divine homage the Persians read into it when it was paid to a favourite lifted into the king's own place.

The puritan Matthew Henry fills in the pressure the courtiers brought to bear. They urged him, he says, reminding him of the king's plain command and of the danger he ran in defying it — it was as much as his life was worth, especially given Haman's known insolence — and they spoke to him daily, hoping to wear down his resolve. But Mordecai would not be moved, and told them roundly that he was a Jew and could not in conscience comply. Henry marks how his neighbours, watching, could not read the refusal aright: some set it down to pride and envy, some to a factious spirit, some more charitably to mere ill-breeding or an affected singularity; not one of them guessed that his standing still while all the rest bowed was itself an act of worship, offered to the God whose honour he would not see given away. Doubtless, Henry observes, the refusal was commonly attributed to his disappointment that his kinship with the queen had not raised him as high as Haman, or to a disaffected and seditious spirit — the very misreadings the world still fastens on those who will not bend where conscience forbids. The reader, who has been told the true reason, is left to watch the informers carry their report to a man whose pride will make the most of it.
4:
The daily questioning hardens into a test. The reformed John Gill notes how the courtiers kept at Mordecai, putting him in mind of his duty, pressing him for his reasons and warning him of his danger; and when he still would not bend, they carried the affair further. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain their motive in a phrase that Charles Ellicott sharpens: they told Haman “to see whether Mordecai's matters would stand” — rather, Ellicott says, whether his words would stand, whether his plea that he belonged to a nation that might pay such reverence to God alone would really hold good. The informers, in other words, were curious to learn whether a religious scruple would prove stronger than a royal edict, and they set the two against each other to find out.

John Wesley reads the same clause to the same end: they reported him “to see” what the event would be, and Scripture adds “for he had told them that he was a Jew” precisely to clear him of the charge of pride — he refused the homage not out of arrogance but out of conscience. The wesleyan and grammatical-historical witnesses thus converge on a single reading of Mordecai's motive, and guard it against the meaner constructions his enemies would soon put upon it. The informers, Keil adds, were testing precisely this — whether a man's religion would really outweigh the king's plain edict — and by carrying the case to Haman rather than letting it lie, they made certain the collision could not be avoided.

The puritan Matthew Henry lingers on the persistence of it all. They spoke to him daily, he says, to persuade him to conform, but all in vain; he hearkened not, but told them plainly that he was a Jew and could not in conscience do it. Here Henry finds the very temper that the citizen of Zion is called to: let those who are governed by principles of conscience be steady and resolute, however they may be censured or threatened. The informers meant their report as mischief, and it would prove so; yet Mordecai's plain confession — repeated day after day, and now carried to the ear of the proud favourite — is the seed from which the whole deliverance of his people will grow, for it fixes the quarrel not on a man's manners but on a Jew's faith. Keil adds the grim sequel the verse only begins: Haman's attention once drawn to the standing figure who would not bow, the stage is set for a wrath out of all proportion to its cause.
5:
Now the favourite looks for himself, and what he sees kindles him. The reformed John Gill notes that after the informers had spoken, Haman watched Mordecai narrowly, marking whether he bowed and did reverence or no; the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add that the next time he went in unto the king and passed the gate, he saw with his own eyes that Mordecai did not fall down before him, and was filled with wrath. The slight was small — one man among a bowing crowd — but Haman's pride made it vast.

The puritan Matthew Henry draws the contrast that the verse invites. A meek and humble man, he says, would have slighted the affront and asked himself what he was the worse for it; he would have let Mordecai keep his humour and thought no more of it. But Haman's proud spirit could not so much as overlook a single unbent knee: it made him rage, and fret, and boil within, till he became a burden to himself and to all about him. Henry reads in this the disease of pride, which cannot bear the least contradiction and turns even its triumphs sour for want of one man's flattery — for Haman had the adoration of a whole empire, and the lack of Mordecai's undid it all. So little, the witnesses imply, can a proud heart enjoy what it holds, while anything it covets remains out of its reach; the one unbent knee spoiled the homage of ten thousand bowed ones.

From that swelling wrath the resolve forms at once. It is soon settled, Henry says, that Mordecai must die: the head that will not bow to Haman must come off; if he cannot have the man's honour he will have his blood. Gill and Keil are content to record the plain fact — that Haman, once his notice had been drawn to the matter, watched and found the affront real, and filled up with wrath — while Henry supplies the moral it carries. The witnesses do not divide over the verse, and their very agreement is the point: that a great officer, lifted above every prince of Persia, should be thrown into a fury by the conscience of a single Jew in the gate is the measure both of Haman's littleness and of the danger now gathering over Mordecai's people. What began as a matter of court etiquette has become, in the heart of a proud man, a matter of life and death; and the next verse will show how far that fury means to reach.
6:
Wrath in a proud man scorns a small revenge, and the witnesses watch Haman's malice widen from one man to a whole nation. The reformed John Gill puts it bluntly: Haman thought it beneath him to lay hands on Mordecai alone, too low and mean a satisfaction for so great an affront; nothing short of the man's whole people would content his vengeance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch say the same — in his pride he esteemed it too contemptible to punish Mordecai only — and note the reason the text gives: “they had shewed him the people of Mordecai,” had told him that as a Jew Mordecai refused, and that the whole Jewish nation held and acted so; wherefore he sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus.

The wesleyan John Wesley traces the springs of so monstrous a leap. Haman thought a narrow vengeance unsuitable to his quality, and he moved against the whole race from an implacable hatred that, as an Amalekite, he bore them of old, from his fresh rage at Mordecai, and from Mordecai's own reason, which, being a Jew, he rightly judged would be shared by every Jew alike. And Wesley marks that the decree would reach even those who had returned to the land of their fathers, for Judea was now but a province of this same empire.

The puritan Matthew Henry gathers the horror and the history together. Haman counts Mordecai's single life nothing toward satisfaction; thousands of innocent and valuable lives must be sacrificed to his indignation, and he vows the destruction of a whole people for one man's sake. Here Henry sees the old antipathy come round again with a terrible symmetry: Saul the son of Kish, a Benjamite, had spared Agag the Amalekite, and now Mordecai the son of Kish, a Benjamite, as ch. 2:5 has told, shall find no mercy from this Agagite; the quarrel God had sworn in Exod. 17:16 and charged Israel to remember in Deut. 25:17 flares up once more. Haman's is the very wish of the enemies in Ps. 83:4, “Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation” — a cruelty, Henry says, like Nero's, that would have all its victims in a single neck. The witnesses do not contend; together they show how a bruised vanity, joined to an ancient hatred, could conceive a whole nation's ruin, and how the refusal of one conscience became the peril of an entire people — a peril, the reader already senses, that the God of that people will not let stand.
7:
Before the plot is laid before the king, it is laid before the lot, and the witnesses read the casting of Pur as a stroke of God's providence disguised as superstition. The reformed John Gill fixes the season — the first month, Nisan, answering to part of our March and April, the opening of the sacred year — and remarks that such exact knowledge of the Jewish calendar shows the book was written by a Jew, most likely Mordecai himself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the practice: to make sure of his great undertaking Haman had recourse to the lot to fix a propitious day, for no weighty thing was attempted in the ancient world without consulting the stars; and the caster is left unnamed because it was plainly some astrologer versed in such arts, before whom, and in whose sight, the lot fell.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke adds from the Greek text what the Hebrew leaves out: the diviners cast, first among the months and then among the days, until the month Adar and a day within it were chosen; and Clarke marvels, half in earnest, whether Haman and his flatterers were already dividing among themselves the spoil of the people they had not yet killed. John Wesley reads the casting as the mark of a settled malice — the diviners sought the luckiest day not for success with the king, of which Haman never doubted, but for the surest extirpation of the Jews — and finds in it, past all Haman's diligence, the singular providence of God, who so disposed the lot that his people should have room to breathe.

For that is the wonder every witness comes to. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the lot fell on the twelfth month, so that nearly a whole year lay between the casting and the intended massacre — time enough, in God's providence, for the matter to be redressed — and he cannot pass Nisan without recalling that it was the Passover month, in which God once spared the blood-marked houses of Israel. The puritan Matthew Henry presses the irony hardest. Haman, eager as he was, would not anticipate his lucky day even to gratify his impatience, but submitted to the laws of his own superstition; and the lot he trusted proved a better friend to the Jews than to him, for by throwing the day eleven months off it gave Mordecai and Esther all that time to defeat the design. “He that believeth the lot,” Henry says, “much more he that believeth the promise, will not make haste”; and he sees God's wisdom serving its own purposes by men's folly, so that Haman, having appealed to the lot, is by the lot condemned, the delay breaking the neck of his plot. The whole scene, Henry adds, opens the doctrine of a particular providence watching over the affairs of men and the safety of the church.
8:
With the day chosen, Haman goes to the king, and the witnesses examine the speech by which he wins his warrant. The reformed John Gill notes a nicety of tense — some render it “Haman had said” — and reasons that he would hardly have cast lots for the day of destruction before he had first obtained the king's leave to destroy at all. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the address and call it very subtly calculated: there is a certain people, Haman says, scattered and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces; their laws are different from those of every other nation; they keep not the king's laws; and therefore it is not for the king's profit to suffer them.

Each clause the witnesses weigh in turn. The one grain of truth in it the wesleyan Adam Clarke fastens on: their laws were indeed diverse from all people, for they worshipped the true God according to his own commandments, which no other nation then on earth did — the very thing that made them precious was turned into their crime. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott exposes the falsehood laid over that truth. The charge of disloyalty, he observes, has always been the persecutor's favourite weapon, and Haman was not the first to level it at the Jews, as Ezra 4:13 shows; our Lord's own accusers would own no king but Caesar, and the early Christians learned how deadly the accusation of disloyalty to the empire could be. Ellicott adds the historical touch that only a part of the nation had returned with Zerubbabel — but 42,360, by Ezra 2:64 — so that the great mass of Jews still lay scattered through the provinces, exactly as Haman said.

The puritan Matthew Henry anatomizes the slander whole. The enemies of God's people, he says, could not treat them so cruelly if they did not first give them a bad name; and Haman's representation has two edges. First, that the Jews are a despicable people, not worth the king's protection — a certain people, nameless, scattered like fugitives and vagabonds, a burden wherever they live. Second, that they are a dangerous people, not safe to keep — having laws of their own and conforming to none of the kingdom's, disaffected to the government and likely to infect others and end in rebellion. It is the common lot of the best of men, Henry reflects, to have such invidious characters fastened on them; and where men think it no sin to kill the innocent, they will think it none to belie them. The witnesses agree that the accusation is a lie wrapped around a truth — a people set apart to God, painted as a people set against the king.
9:
Haman's proposal comes with a price attached, and the witnesses divide their attention between the cruelty of the request and the vastness of the bribe. The reformed John Gill reads the petition plainly: let a law be made, signed and sealed, and letters sent everywhere ordering the Jews' destruction. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the terms in full — if it please the king, let it be written that they be destroyed, and Haman will weigh ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those that do the business, to be brought into the king's treasuries.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke marks the cunning of the wording. By asking that it be written, that it pass into a law, Haman throws the odium off himself and onto the king and his counsellors, keeping for himself only a small share of the blame. And Clarke reckons the offered sum, which he owns to be immense — some two millions sterling and more — against the scoffers who would call such wealth in a single subject incredible, marshalling Herodotus and Plutarch to show that private men of the ancient world did hold fortunes as great; the money was no fable. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the figure in proportion: ten thousand talents was near two and a half millions of our money, more than two-thirds of the whole yearly revenue of the empire, so that either Haman was a man of enormous wealth or, more likely, he counted on repaying himself out of the plunder of his victims.

That last suspicion the puritan Matthew Henry shares and drives home. Haman bids high, he says, because he knows how many already hate the Jews and will fall on them gladly once the word is given; and the ten thousand talents are meant to answer the one objection a king might raise, that his revenue must suffer by the loss of so many subjects. But proud and malicious men will not stick at the expense of their revenge — and in truth Haman meant to be no loser, for he knew how to reimburse himself from the spoil of the Jews, which his agents were to seize by the terms of v.13, making the victims bear the very cost of their own ruin while he came off a gainer. The witnesses do not quarrel; they agree that the offer was at once a mask, to hide the author of the slaughter, and a lure, to buy a king's consent — and that the money, whatever its source, was to be squeezed in the end from the blood of the innocent.
10:
The king's answer is wordless at first — he simply takes off his ring — and the witnesses see in that small gesture the whole weight of an empire signed away. The reformed John Gill explains that among the Persians for a king to give his ring was the token and bond of the greatest love and friendship; here it was handed over that Haman might seal with it the letters ordering the destruction of the Jews. And Gill draws a shrewd inference from the ease of it: surely Esther had not yet told the king who her kindred and people were, for otherwise he could hardly have handed her enemy so free a warrant.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the act's legal force. The king drew the signet from his hand and gave it to Haman that he might draft the edict in the king's own name and, by the impress of the royal seal, give it the authority of a decree that could not be revoked; and they note how pointedly the text names the man who received it — “the Jews' enemy,” set down with deliberate emphasis. The wesleyan Adam Clarke fills in the custom: the ring carried the privy seal, and with it whatever Haman chose to write would have full force among the governors of the provinces; the seals of Eastern kings were worn so, upon the finger, ready to stamp a despatch at a moment's will.

The puritan Matthew Henry turns the transaction into an indictment of the king. Ahasuerus was so heedless of his business, and so bewitched with his favourite, that he took no time to examine the truth of Haman's charge, but gave up a whole people into his hands as lambs to the lion, and with them his ring to confirm the deed. Miserable, Henry cries, is the kingdom at the disposal of such a head — a head with one ear only, and a nose to be led by, but neither eyes to see nor brains to weigh what it does. The witnesses stand together in their alarm: the mightiest instrument of the realm, the seal that turned Haman's malice into irrevocable law, was surrendered in a moment, without inquiry, to the one man in the empire least fit to hold it — and the reader, who knows what Ahasuerus does not, watches an enemy of God's people arm himself with a king's own authority.
11:
The king's one speech in the whole transaction is a careless generosity, and the witnesses hear in it both indifference and a kind of studied face-saving. The reformed John Gill takes “the silver is given to thee” to mean that the ten thousand talents were returned, the king out of his great munificence refusing to take the money. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the gesture more warily: lest it should appear that a bribe had moved him, the king makes over the silver to Haman — “the silver be given to thee, and the people, to do with them as seemeth good to thee” — so that the refusal is less munificence than a screen for his own complicity.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the whole reply incredible and yet entirely in character with what is known of Xerxes: with an indifference that beggars belief, the king hands over a whole nation and all its possessions to his minister, to do with as he pleases. Perhaps, Ellicott suggests, he was glad to be rid of the cares of government, and, too indolent to form a judgment of his own, was content to believe the Jews the worthless, disloyal people Haman had painted them. The silver he waves aside with a phrase and the people he gives away in the same breath, as though a nation's life weighed no more with him than the sum he had just declined to take.

The puritan Matthew Henry joins the same threads into a portrait of reckless misrule. The king, he says, does not so much as say “kill them” — perhaps hoping Haman's cooler thoughts would abate the sentence and sell the people for slaves rather than slay them — but says only, “Do with them as it seemeth good unto thee,” and gives him the silver too, so little did he consider what his treasury would lose or his favourite gain. It is the abandonment of a whole people to a private malice, ratified with a shrug. The witnesses do not finally divide over whether the king truly declined the money or merely made a show of declining it; they agree on the thing that matters — that Ahasuerus gave away the lives of his innocent subjects more easily than most men would give away a trifle, and that the fate of a nation now hung upon the whim of a king who would not trouble himself to ask whether the charge against them was even true.
12:
The machinery of a world-empire is now turned to a single murderous end, and the witnesses trace the paperwork with care. The reformed John Gill notes the date — the thirteenth day of the first month, Nisan — when the king's scribes, his secretaries of state, were summoned to write the letters. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch spread out the full apparatus: it was written according to all that Haman commanded, to the king's satraps, to the governors set over every province, and to the rulers of every people, each province in its own script and each people in its own tongue; in the name of King Ahasuerus it was written, and sealed with the king's ring — the whole vast administrative net of Persia drawn tight to catch one small nation.

The witnesses pause over the officers named. Adam Clarke observes that “the king's lieutenants” renders a Persian word, the satraps, which the Hebrew only transliterates; and Charles Ellicott confirms it — the term behind “lieutenants” is the Persian original that passed through Greek into our own word satrap, and it recurs across this book and Ezra and Daniel. The care taken to reach every province in its own writing and language, both grammatical-historical witnesses note, shows how the decree was meant to leave no corner of the realm and no community of Jews beyond its reach.

Ellicott lingers on the date with a longer view. The thirteenth of Adar was to be the fatal day, and that, he suggests, may be why the thirteenth of Nisan was chosen for this first step; but he cannot let the day pass without recalling, with Bishop Wordsworth, that it was the eve of the Passover. So Haman's plot against the Jews strangely fell in the same season as another assault five hundred years later, when the powers of darkness and heathen hands sought to destroy the Saviour; and as the trembling Jews of Persia were delivered by the goodness of God, so by that same goodness the greater enemy was in time overthrown. The witnesses do not divide; together they show a whole imperial system — scribes, satraps, seal, and the swift tongues of many nations — bent to write into irrevocable law the ruin of a people whose only crime was that one of them would bow to God alone. The very thoroughness of the edict, drawn in the king's name and sealed with his ring, is what will make its later reversal so signal a mercy.
13:
The letters go out, and the witnesses dwell both on the speed that carried them and the savagery they carried. The reformed John Gill describes the posts — the runners, or rather the mounted couriers the Persians called angari, a relay of horses and riders stationed at intervals, the swiftest dispatch the ancient world knew, whom neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness could stay from their course. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the system from Herodotus — the post-riders set some four parasangs apart along the royal roads — and then give the letters' dreadful content: to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish all Jews, young and old, little children and women, in one day, the thirteenth of Adar, and to take their goods for a spoil. The three verbs are heaped together, Keil notes, for sheer force, and the plunder is named to whet the killers' greed.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke reads the same clause and sees the machinery of a general massacre: the Jews were to be put to death by any hand and every means, and whoever killed a Jew was to have his property for the trouble — so that every man's covetousness was armed against them. Clarke recalls that the Greek and Latin texts preserve the decree at length, in which the king professes a care for the peace of his realm and denounces a detestable people, scattered everywhere, who keep their own laws and change the king's, and whose utter extermination, root and branch, male and female, young and old, alone can secure the public quiet.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds only that “posts” means the runners, the royal couriers of the empire. The witnesses do not divide; they set the wonder of Persia's swift and orderly government against the wickedness it was here made to serve, and let the horror of the edict speak for itself. Nothing in it is left to chance or mercy: a fixed day, a whole people, every age and both sexes, and a bounty of plunder to make neighbours into executioners. It is the church's old enemy, Gill and Clarke alike imply, thirsting after the blood of the innocent; and the reader, holding in mind that the day is eleven months off and the God of the Jews not asleep, is meant to feel at once the full weight of the danger and the narrow, providential space still left for deliverance.
14:
The decree is not only sent but published, and the witnesses ask what that publication meant. The reformed John Gill explains that besides the sealed letters to the governors, a copy or summary of their contents was proclaimed by heralds and posted up in the open, that the common people everywhere might know what was coming and hold themselves in readiness for it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the word: this is no mere allusion to the letter already sent, but the historical notice that the copy dispatched into every province was galui — opened, sent unsealed and uncovered — so that a law might be given, and given openly, to all peoples, that they should be ready against the appointed day.

Charles Ellicott adds a word on the term rendered “copy,” the Persian pathshegen, which meets us only here and twice more in the book. Keil is careful to say that the verse announces no fresh proclamation of the sort found among the decrees of Ezra, but simply records that the writing sent as law into the provinces was left open, that its contents and its purpose might be known to every people. The point on which the grammatical-historical witnesses agree is the strange openness of the thing: the order was not whispered but broadcast, published to the very people among whom the Jews lived, and published eleven months before it was to be executed, so that every province might arm itself in good time.

That openness is itself the horror the verse quietly holds. A whole population is told in advance to make ready for a massacre; the intended victims must live out nearly a year knowing the day of their appointed slaughter, and their neighbours are put on notice to prepare their hands for it. Yet the witnesses let the reader see, without labouring it, how the same openness that seemed to seal the Jews' doom would serve their rescue: a decree published so widely and so early could be answered, in God's time, by a counter-decree published as widely, and the long interval the tyrant allowed for his cruelty became the very space in which mercy could work. What was meant to give the whole empire time to sharpen its knives gave the appointed victims time to be delivered. The bare administrative notice — that the writing was “opened” to all people — thus carries, under its officialdom, both the reach of the danger and the seed of its undoing.
15:
The chapter closes on a single, terrible contrast, and every witness feels it. The reformed John Gill notes the haste — the posts went out driven by the king's command, to set off and make all speed — and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch complete the scene: the couriers hurried forth at the royal word, the decree was promulgated in the citadel of Susa, and then the king and Haman sat down together to drink, while the city of Susa was thrown into perplexity. The word for that perplexity, Keil observes, is the same used of a people bewildered and dismayed, as in Joel 1:18; the cruel measure filled every peace-loving citizen with horror.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke enlarges on the city's alarm. The people of Susa saw that in a short time the whole city would be flung into confusion, for though the Jews alone were named, a decree that armed the mob against them endangered all: once a desperate rabble had tasted blood and plunder, no Persian family could be sure of safety, and many were joined to Jews by marriage and would share their fate. Clarke can hardly contain his indignation — a more impolitic, disgraceful, and cruel measure, he says, was never framed by any government; the king who ordered it must have been an idiot and his counsellors madmen, for despotism is forever capable of such extravagance, the standing curse of a nation. John Wesley reads the city's grief more tenderly: not the Jews only were troubled, but a great number of the citizens, whether from kinship, or common dealings, or plain humanity toward so vast a multitude of innocent people appointed, like sheep, for the slaughter.

Charles Ellicott hears in the city's dismay a verdict on Haman: the people of the capital were puzzled and alarmed at so reckless an order, and their sympathies were plainly with the Jews and against the man who had contrived it. The puritan Matthew Henry draws the closing contrast to its point. The court is merry and the city sad: the king and Haman sit down to drink, perhaps to toast the ruin of the Jews, and Haman keeps the king at the cup, Henry suspects, lest his conscience should wake and he repent the deed — the cursed method by which many still drown their convictions and harden their own hearts and others' in sin. Meanwhile the city grieves to see its king so abused and wickedness set in the place of judgment. It is an absurd and impious thing, Henry warns, to give ourselves up to mirth and pleasure while the church is in distress; and the two tables — the king's wine and the city's dread — are the last image the chapter leaves us, callous power feasting above, helpless innocence trembling below, and, unseen by either, the God who will overturn the one to save the other.
